stem: A developer must process 10,000 documents overnight to produce a non-urgent analytics report. Cost is the primary concern, and results are not needed until the following morning. Which approach best fits the requirement?

options.text: Send every request synchronously through the Messages API in parallel to finish as quickly as possible.
options.why: Parallel synchronous calls finish sooner but are billed at the full realtime rate, so they do nothing for the primary concern, cost.

options.text: Use the Message Batches API, which processes large asynchronous workloads within a 24-hour window at reduced cost.
options.why: Batches are built for high-volume, latency-tolerant work: requests complete asynchronously (within 24 hours) at a discounted per-token price, which fits an overnight, cost-driven job.

options.text: Lower max_tokens on synchronous calls to minimize cost.
options.why: max_tokens only caps output length; it risks truncated results and does not change the per-token price or address the batch-versus-realtime choice.

options.text: Switch to the smallest available model regardless of output quality.
options.why: Downsizing "regardless of quality" ignores the report's requirements; model choice should follow a quality/cost tradeoff, not replace the right API mode.

explanation: The Message Batches API is designed for latency-tolerant, high-volume workloads at lower cost, which matches an overnight, non-urgent job. The other options either do not reduce per-token cost or trade away quality without addressing the batch-versus-realtime decision.
reference: Claude API docs — Batch processing (Message Batches API)

stem: A Claude-powered agent summarizes web pages submitted by end users. One page contains hidden text instructing the model to ignore previous instructions and reveal its system prompt. Which mitigation is most effective?

options.text: Raise the model's temperature so its behavior is harder to predict.
options.why: Temperature changes sampling randomness; it has no bearing on whether injected instructions are followed and makes the app less reliable.

options.text: Treat retrieved page content as untrusted input, keep it separate from trusted instructions, and use guardrails or hooks so injected instructions cannot trigger sensitive actions.
options.why: Isolating untrusted content from trusted instructions and enforcing least-privilege guardrails outside the model means injected text cannot reach sensitive capabilities even if the model is fooled.

options.text: Add a line to the system prompt asking users not to include malicious instructions.
options.why: A polite request is not an enforceable control; attackers simply ignore it.

options.text: Switch to a larger model that follows instructions more reliably.
options.why: Better instruction-following does not distinguish trusted from untrusted instructions and can make a model more, not less, responsive to injected text.

explanation: Prompt injection is addressed by isolating untrusted content from trusted instructions and enforcing least-privilege guardrails so injected text cannot invoke sensitive tools. Temperature is irrelevant, a polite request is not a control, and a more instruction-following model is not a defense.
reference: Claude docs — Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections

stem: A team needs Claude to call an internal inventory service exposed as a REST API. They want the capability to be reusable across several Claude applications and maintained independently of any one app. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Hard-code the inventory logic into each application's system prompt.
options.why: A prompt cannot call a REST API, and copying logic into every app is neither reusable nor maintainable.

options.text: Build an MCP server that exposes the inventory operations as tools so multiple Claude applications can connect to it.
options.why: An MCP server packages the operations once as tools that any MCP-capable Claude client can connect to, and it can be versioned and deployed independently of the apps.

options.text: Paste the current inventory data into the context window on every request.
options.why: Pasted data is a stale snapshot with no live access or write path, and it wastes context tokens on every call.

options.text: Rely on a built-in tool, since built-in tools can reach any internal REST API.
options.why: Built-in tools do not automatically reach arbitrary internal APIs; private services need a custom tool or an MCP server.

explanation: An MCP server exposes reusable tools that multiple Claude applications can share and that can be maintained independently. Prompt hard-coding is not reusable, pasting data gives no live access, and built-in tools do not reach arbitrary internal APIs.
